title: He Roamed in Search of Safety
intro: A mother tries to learn from her absent son's silence how he died. Al-Tabrizi favours the attribution to al-Sulaka, mother of the famous runner al-Sulayk, while al-Farisi records other names. She speaks of him at first, then addresses him directly until the questions give way to a wish that she had died before him.

translation: He roamed in search of safety
from destruction, and perished.
1.sharh: He keeps moving in search of a way out. “Safety” can suggest ground high enough to escape a flood. Al-Tabrizi understands the danger that drove him out as poverty.

translation: If only I knew, lost as I am,
what it was that killed you.
2.sharh: She changes from “he” to “you”. His death is certain enough for lament, yet the circumstances are so obscure that she still addresses him as her best witness.

translation: Were you ill, with no one to visit you,
or did an enemy take you unawares?
3.sharh: She imagines two kinds of loneliness. In one he sickens with no visitor at his bedside. In the other someone has watched for the chance to catch him off guard.

translation: Or were you carried off by what
has snatched partridge chicks away down the years?
4.sharh: The bird's name, sulak, echoes Sulayk. The runner she knew for his speed becomes as vulnerable as the young bird swept away in an instant.

translation: Deaths lie in wait
for a young man wherever he goes.
5.sharh: Death waits along every route he might take. Her son's roaming in the opening now looks like movement between places where the same pursuer is already waiting.

translation: What fine quality
could a young man have that you lacked?
6.sharh: She cannot think of an admirable quality in a young man that was missing in him. For a moment, naming what he was takes the place of guessing how he died.

translation: Anything can kill you
when your time has come.
7.sharh: She has been weighing one possible cause against another. Once his allotted time arrived even an ordinary thing could have been enough.

translation: How often you won
your heart's desire without a struggle.
8.sharh: He used to reach the thing he set his heart on with such ease. That memory makes his failure to come back from this journey harder for her to grasp.

translation: Something terrible indeed
kept you from answering me.
9.sharh: She treats his silence as an interruption, almost as if he might still speak once the terrible business is over. The understatement lets the listener hear the loss.

translation: I will try to console myself, since
you give the one who asks no answer.
10.sharh: She takes his failure to answer as her cue to attempt consolation. The future tense leaves room for the wishes that follow.

translation: If only for one hour my heart
could command its patience at losing you.
11.sharh: She asks for control of her grief for a single hour. Even that small interval of composure feels beyond her power.

translation: If only my own life had been sent
to meet death ahead of you.
12.sharh: Her last wish rewinds the order of their deaths. The reciter's “before you” makes the unbearable fact that she has survived her son the last thing we hear.

1.1.3.head: نَجوَة
1.1.3.meaning: Safety or escape. The concrete sense is high ground beyond a flood's reach.

1.2.2.head: هَلاك
1.2.2.meaning: Ruin or mortal danger, taken by al-Tabrizi as destitution.

2.1.1-2.meaning: “If only I knew”, a formula for longing to know something out of reach.

2.1.3.head: ضَلَّة
2.1.3.meaning: Bewilderment, being at a loss for an explanation.

3.1.3.head: عادَ
3.1.3.meaning: Be visited in sickness. She imagines an illness borne alone.

3.2.3.head: خَتَلَ
3.2.3.meaning: Caught you unawares by stealth or deception.

4.2.4.meaning: Sulak, a young partridge. Sulayk is the diminutive of the same word.

5.1.2.head: رَصَد
5.1.2.meaning: Watchers lying in wait for a passer-by.

6.2.3.head: كانَ
6.2.3.meaning: A shortened form of “be” after a negative, here “did you not have”.

9.1.3.head: فادِح
9.1.3.meaning: Crushing, a burden too heavy to bear.

10.1.1.head: عَزّى
10.1.1.meaning: I shall try to console, here to steady herself after loss.

11.2.1.head: صَبر
11.2.1.meaning: Its capacity to bear the loss and hold grief in check.

12.2.1.head: المَنايا
12.2.1.meaning: The deaths allotted to human beings.

12.2.2.head: قِبَل
12.2.2.meaning: Ahead of you. Usaylan prints the word recited here. His apparatus and al-Tabrizi also give badalak, “in your stead”.
